title: Bernoulli and binomial sampling models
dek: A Bernoulli is one 0/1 trial with mean π. A binomial is the sum of n independent Bernoulli trials — or a single count with that same law. Most resistance proportions start here.
story: A Bernoulli random variable Y takes values 0 or 1 with P(Y = 1) = π and P(Y = 0) = 1 − π. Then E[Y] = π and Var(Y) = π(1 − π). A smear-positive indicator, a high-confidence gyrA call, a culture conversion by month two: each is a Bernoulli the moment you write that mean.

If Y₁, …, Yₙ are iid Bernoulli(π), their sum X = ∑ Yᵢ is Binomial(n, π): P(X = k) = C(n,k) π^k (1−π)^{n−k} for k = 0, …, n. The mean is nπ and the variance is nπ(1−π). The sample proportion π̂ = X/n is the MLE and is also Ȳ. Same likelihood, two fonts.

Independence is doing the heavy lifting. n isolates from one outbreak are not n Bernoulli trials of a population proportion. Overdispersed binary data (households, labs) need a Beta-Binomial, a mixed logit, or a sandwich — not a smaller p-value from pretending n grew.
deep: Log-likelihood ℓ(π) = x log π + (n − x) log(1 − π) (plus the binomial coefficient, which does not depend on π). Score x/π − (n−x)/(1−π) = 0 recovers π̂ = x/n. Fisher information n/(π(1−π)) is smallest near 0 and 1 — rare alleles are poorly estimated because the curvature vanishes, not because the sequencer failed.

Normal approximation: for nπ and n(1−π) both comfortably large, X is approximately N(nπ, nπ(1−π)) and π̂ is approximately N(π, π(1−π)/n). Wald intervals π̂ ± 1.96 se fail near 0 and 1. Score and Clopper–Pearson intervals exist because this approximation is a tool, not a right.
Poisson limit: if n → ∞, π → 0, nπ → λ, then X →d Poisson(λ). Rare adverse events and sparse mutation counts sometimes prefer that limit as the working law.

Binomial versus Bernoulli GLM: nᵢ trials at covariate pattern i with yᵢ successes is the same exponential family as nᵢ rows of Bernoulli. Grouping changes the residual df and the Pearson dispersion check; it does not change the MLE of a shared π.
Negative binomial is not “the other binomial.” It is an overdispersed count law (own plate). Do not relabel a binomial because the Pearson χ² looked large — write the extra-dispersion model.

visual.caption: Three binomial laws with n = 20. Mean nπ moves the mass; variance nπ(1−π) is largest near π = 0.5 and collapses toward 0 and 1. That collapse is why rare-resistance intervals are awkward, not a software bug.

example.title: FQ-R among 50 RR isolates
example.setup: n = 50 sequenced RR-TB isolates, x = 8 with a high-confidence gyrA QRDR mutation. Working model: X ~ Binomial(50, π). Estimate π and quote Var(π̂) at the MLE.

steps.title: MLE
steps.body: π̂ = 8/50 = 0.16. This is also the sample mean of 50 Bernoulli indicators.

steps.title: Variance of the count and of the proportion
When the model is the lie
steps.body: If 20 of the 50 are a single L2 outbreak clone, n is not 50 independent Bernoulli trials. Report a cluster-robust or hierarchical variance, not a smaller binomial p-value.

example.takeaway: Write n, π, and the independence claim. The binomial is a joint, not a histogram bin.

check.prompt: A Binomial(n, π) count is the sampling law of:
choices: Any 0/1 column in a spreadsheet, even if rows are clustered
The sum of n independent Bernoulli(π) trials (or an equivalent single-count model)
check.answer: The sum of n independent Bernoulli(π) trials (or an equivalent single-count model)
check.why: The binomial coefficient and the π^k (1−π)^{n−k} form come from independent identical Bernoulli trials.

whyWrong.Any 0/1 column in a spreadsheet, even if: Clustering breaks independence; the pmf is then wrong.
whyWrong.A Normal with mean π: That is an approximation for π̂, not the exact law of one trial.
whyWrong.A Poisson regardless of π: Poisson is a limit for rare events, not the exact binomial.

check.prompt: X ~ Binomial(n=10, π=0.3). What is Var(X)?
check.why: nπ(1−π) = 10×0.3×0.7 = 2.1. The mean is 3; the variance is not.

whyWrong.0.3: That is π, not a variance of the count.
whyWrong.7: That is n(1−π), not the variance.

check.prompt: On the small-multiples plate, why is the middle panel (π = 0.5) the most spread out?
choices: Because n is largest in the middle panel
Because π(1−π) is maximised at π = 0.5, so the binomial variance nπ(1−π) is largest there
Because binomial laws are always symmetric
check.answer: Because π(1−π) is maximised at π = 0.5, so the binomial variance nπ(1−π) is largest there
check.why: The quadratic π(1−π) peaks at one half. Near 0 or 1 the mass piles at the edge.

whyWrong.Because MLE is undefined at 0.5: The MLE is Ȳ, defined on (0,1) and at the boundary as 0 or 1.
